knowledge_meta.name: Professional & Engineering Services
knowledge_meta.description: Digital consulting, software engineering services, project-based delivery organisations. Covers project portfolio management, resource utilisation, timesheet-based billing, presales pipeline, and financial forecasting.
typical_organisations: Professional services divisions within larger companies

phases.name: Business Questions
phases.description: Identify the top financial questions leadership needs answered each period

questions.text: What are the top 3 financial questions your leadership team asks each month or quarter?
follow_ups: How quickly do you need those answers — same day, within a week, or is month-end reporting sufficient?
Who specifically asks these questions — CFO, MD, board?
hints: Common in services: 'What's our gross margin per project?', 'Are we on budget?', 'What does our pipeline look like?'
Revenue recognition timing is often a pain point — when does revenue get recognised vs when work is done?
Ask about the difference between forecast and actuals — services firms often struggle with forecast accuracy

questions.text: How do you measure project profitability? Is it per-project, per-account, per-practice, or all three?
follow_ups: Do you use blended day rates or actual salary costs?
Are tool/licence costs allocated to projects or kept as overheads?
hints: Gross margin = (Revenue - Direct Costs) / Revenue. Direct costs typically = people cost (blended rate × days)
Some firms also allocate licence costs, travel, and subcontractor costs per project
Blended rates vs actual costs: blended is simpler but hides margin distortion from seniority mix

questions.text: What financial reports does your finance team produce each period? Walk me through the month-end close.
follow_ups: How many days after month-end do you have final numbers?
What's the biggest bottleneck in the close process?
hints: Common bottleneck: timesheet approval — PMs haven't approved timesheets so finance can't post actuals
Oracle/ERP actuals often lag 5-10 working days after month-end
Variance analysis (budget vs actual vs forecast) is typically the most time-consuming step
Portfolio-level consolidation often involves manual Excel compilation across projects

questions.text: How do you forecast revenue and costs? Is it bottom-up from project forecasts or top-down from targets?
follow_ups: How often are forecasts updated?
Do PMs own their forecasts or does finance create them?
hints: Bottom-up: PM forecasts hours remaining × rate = cost forecast. More accurate but depends on PM discipline
Top-down: finance sets targets and allocates. Faster but disconnected from project reality
Common pain: PM forecasts live in Excel, not in the project management tool. Version control issues
Forecast vs budget vs actuals is the triangle — most firms struggle to get all three in one view

common_metrics.name: Revenue & Gross Margin
common_metrics.business_question: Are we profitable? What's our margin per project/account?

common_metrics.name: Budget Adherence
common_metrics.business_question: Are we spending within approved budgets?

common_metrics.name: Forecast Accuracy
common_metrics.business_question: Can we trust our forecasts for planning decisions?

common_metrics.name: Pipeline Health
common_metrics.business_question: Do we have enough pipeline to sustain future revenue?

phases.name: Metric Definition
phases.description: Turn business questions into precise metric definitions with clear ownership

questions.text: For each financial question you mentioned, let's define exactly what 'good' looks like. What are your targets or benchmarks?
follow_ups: Are these targets set annually, quarterly, or per-project?
Who is accountable for each metric?
hints: Typical services benchmarks: 30-40% gross margin, 75-85% utilisation, <5% budget variance
Pipeline coverage ratio: typically 3x next quarter's revenue target
Forecast accuracy: top-quartile firms achieve ±5% by month 2 of quarter

questions.text: When you say 'profitability', what costs do you include? Just people, or also tools, travel, subcontractors?
follow_ups: Do you distinguish between gross margin and contribution margin?
Are there different profitability views for different audiences?
hints: Gross margin: Revenue - Direct People Cost
Contribution margin: Revenue - All Direct Costs (people + tools + travel + subs)
Net margin: After overhead allocation — useful but often contentious methodology
Most services firms start with gross margin as the primary profitability metric

phases.name: Measure Tracing
phases.description: Trace each metric back to the calculations and data it requires

questions.text: Let's trace your profitability metric. Revenue comes from where — your ERP/GL? And costs?
follow_ups: Is revenue recognised on invoice, on timesheet approval, or on milestone completion?
Are there revenue adjustments or accruals that complicate this?
hints: Revenue recognition method matters enormously: time & materials (simpler) vs fixed-price (requires % complete)
People cost = blended day rate × approved days. Where does the blended rate come from?
Watch for: rate changes mid-project, different rates for different clients, on-shore vs off-shore rates

questions.text: For budget variance, where is the approved budget stored? And how do actuals flow in?
follow_ups: Can the budget change after approval, or is it locked?
How do change requests affect the budget?
hints: Budget is often set at SOW signing and stored in the project management tool
Actuals typically come from the GL/ERP after month-end posting
The gap between 'actuals available' and 'budget approved' is where variance analysis happens
Change requests that modify budget are a common source of confusion — is it a new budget or a variance?

phases.name: Data Sourcing
phases.description: Identify exactly where the data lives and how reliable it is

questions.text: For each data point we've identified, which system is the source of truth? And is that system actually used, or do people use Excel instead?
follow_ups: Are there reconciliation processes between systems?
What happens when the system data doesn't match Excel?
hints: Common pattern: ERP is 'official' source but Excel is 'real' source. Flag this as a shadow system risk
Project management tools (Mieruka, Jira, Monday, Smartsheet) often have data quality issues because PMs don't update them
HR systems (HiBob, BambooHR, Workday) are usually reliable for leave/availability but not integrated with project tools
Finance systems (Oracle, SAP, Xero, NetSuite) are source of truth for actuals but lag behind reality

questions.text: How much of your financial reporting is manual? Roughly what percentage of time is spent gathering data vs analysing it?
follow_ups: Are there specific steps that are particularly painful or error-prone?
If you could automate one thing, what would have the biggest impact?
hints: 80/20 rule: most finance teams spend 80% gathering and 20% analysing. The goal is to flip this
System switching (Oracle → Excel → PowerPoint → Email) is the biggest waste category in services
Monthly portfolio reports that take 2+ days to compile are a strong automation candidate
Look for: manual data re-entry, copy-paste between systems, emailed spreadsheets as data transfer

typical_systems.name: ERP / General Ledger
typical_systems.role: Financial system of record — revenue recognition, cost posting, actuals
common_issues: Chart of accounts may not map cleanly to project structure

typical_systems.name: Project Management / PSA
typical_systems.role: Project tracking, resource allocation, budgets, timesheets
common_issues: Data staleness — PMs don't update regularly

typical_systems.name: Development / Delivery Tools
typical_systems.role: Sprint tracking, story points, task management, time logging (granular)
common_issues: Not all teams use time logging
Story point calibration varies across teams

phases.name: Monitoring & KPIs
phases.description: Understand what management monitors and how they know if things are on track

questions.text: As a manager, what do you check first thing Monday morning to know if things are on track?
follow_ups: How do you currently get this information — dashboard, email, meeting, or manual check?
What would you ideally see that you can't see today?
hints: Common: project RAG status, utilisation this week, overdue timesheets, pipeline movement
The gap between 'what I check' and 'what I'd like to check' reveals missing metrics
If the answer is 'I check Slack/Teams messages' — that's tribal knowledge, not a system

questions.text: How do you know if a project is in trouble? What are the early warning signs?
follow_ups: At what point do you escalate — what triggers that decision?
Is there a formal RAG status process, or is it informal?
hints: Early warning signs: sprint velocity declining, burn rate exceeding plan, key resource departure, scope creep
RAG status is often subjective — PMs self-assess. Ask if there are objective criteria
Escalation triggers: >10% budget variance, missed milestone, client complaint, resource gap
The time between 'problem appears' and 'management knows' is the observability gap

questions.text: How do you track resource utilisation? What's your target, and how close do you get?
follow_ups: Is utilisation measured weekly, monthly, or quarterly?
Do you distinguish between billable and non-billable utilisation?
hints: Utilisation = Billable Hours / Available Hours. Typical target: 75-85%
Available hours must account for leave, public holidays, training, internal work
Common pain: utilisation data requires combining project tool (allocation) + HR tool (leave) + timesheet (actuals)
Bench time (unallocated resources) is the inverse of utilisation — both views are valuable

questions.text: How do you monitor the presales pipeline? What visibility do you have into future work?
follow_ups: How do you weight pipeline opportunities — by probability, by stage, or gut feel?
What's your pipeline coverage ratio target (pipeline ÷ quarterly revenue target)?
hints: Pipeline stages: Lead → Qualified → Proposal → Negotiation → Won/Lost
Weighted pipeline = Σ(deal value × probability). Unweighted overestimates future revenue
Conversion rate by stage helps identify where deals get stuck
Pipeline-to-revenue lag: how long from 'won' to 'first revenue'? This affects capacity planning

common_metrics.name: Project Delivery Performance
common_metrics.business_question: Are we delivering what we committed to?

common_metrics.name: Resource Utilisation Rate
common_metrics.business_question: Are our people fully utilised, or do we have idle capacity?

common_metrics.name: Timesheet Compliance
common_metrics.business_question: Are timesheets being submitted and approved on time?

common_metrics.name: Portfolio Risk Exposure
common_metrics.business_question: What is our aggregate risk across all projects?

phases.name: Connect Up to Financial
phases.description: Link management KPIs to the financial metrics they feed

questions.text: Which of your management KPIs directly impact financial outcomes? For example, does low utilisation directly reduce margin?
follow_ups: Can you quantify the financial impact — e.g., each 1% utilisation drop costs £X?
Are there leading indicators that predict financial problems before they show up in the P&L?
hints: Utilisation → Revenue (fewer billable days = less revenue)
Budget variance → Profitability (overspend reduces margin)
Pipeline health → Future revenue (weak pipeline = revenue gap in 3-6 months)
Timesheet compliance → Financial reporting speed (late timesheets delay month-end close)

questions.text: When finance asks you for data at month-end, what do they need and how do you provide it?
follow_ups: Is this a pull (they extract from systems) or a push (you send them reports)?
What format — Excel, system export, verbal update?
hints: Common: finance needs approved timesheets, forecast updates, and budget change requests
The handoff between management and finance is often the biggest bottleneck in month-end close
If the answer is 'I email them an Excel file' — that's a crystallisation point worth capturing

phases.name: Connect Down to Operational
phases.description: Link management monitoring to the operational data it depends on

questions.text: What data do you need from your delivery teams to do your job? Think about what you chase people for.
follow_ups: How reliable is the data you get — do you trust it or verify it?
What's the lag — how quickly does operational data reach you?
hints: Common: sprint progress from Jira, timesheets from PSA tool, risk updates from PMs
Trust issues often stem from: data entered retrospectively, aggregated instead of granular, self-reported
The lag between 'event happens' and 'manager sees it' determines decision speed

questions.text: How do you allocate resources to projects? Walk me through what happens when a new project starts.
follow_ups: Can you allocate someone to multiple projects simultaneously?
What happens when demand exceeds capacity — how do you prioritise?
hints: Resource allocation is often the most painful process in services firms
Common issue: PSA tool only allows one project per person, so real allocation is in Excel
Fractional allocation (0.5 FTE on Project A, 0.3 on B, 0.2 on C) is common but hard to track
HiBob/BambooHR availability data often not integrated with project allocation tools
The gap between 'official allocation' and 'actual work being done' is a key data quality risk

phases.name: Pain Points & Workarounds
phases.description: Identify where management work is painful, manual, or relies on workarounds

questions.text: What's the most time-consuming part of your week that you wish was automated or simpler?
follow_ups: How many hours per week do you spend on this?
Have you tried to fix it before — what happened?
hints: Status reporting typically takes PMs 1-2 hours per project per week — across 5 projects that's a full day
Resource allocation reviews often require checking 3+ systems (PSA, HR, Excel)
Chasing timesheets is a common time sink — especially at month-end
Forecast updates often require re-building Excel models from scratch each month

questions.text: Are there any Excel spreadsheets that your team couldn't function without? What do they track that your systems can't?
follow_ups: Who maintains these spreadsheets?
How many people have access to the 'real' version?
hints: Shadow systems in Excel are the #1 data quality risk in services firms
Common shadow spreadsheets: resource allocation tracker, project forecast model, pipeline tracker, rate card
These exist because the official tools can't do: multi-project allocation, granular forecasting, flexible reporting
Each shadow spreadsheet is a candidate for 'what should the system do that it doesn't'

typical_systems.name: HR / People System
typical_systems.role: Employee data, leave/time-off, availability, org structure

typical_systems.name: Communication / Collaboration
common_issues: Key decisions made in chat but not documented

phases.name: Systems & People
phases.description: Map the systems people use daily and who uses them

questions.text: Walk me through a typical day for someone on your delivery team. What systems do they touch?
follow_ups: In what order do they use these systems?
Are there any systems they're supposed to use but often skip?
hints: Typical developer day: Jira (check tasks) → IDE (code) → Git (commit) → Jira (update) → Slack/Teams (communicate) → PSA tool (log time, maybe)
Typical PM day: Email → PSA tool (check status) → Jira (review progress) → Excel (update forecast) → Teams (meetings) → PSA tool (approve timesheets)
Systems they 'skip' reveal data gaps — if developers don't log time in Jira, granular effort data is missing

questions.text: Who are the key roles in your delivery process? List them from most client-facing to most internal.
follow_ups: Which roles create the most data? Which roles consume the most reports?
Are there any roles that bridge multiple teams or systems?
hints: Common services roles: Account Manager, Project Manager, Scrum Master, Tech Lead, Developer, QA, Designer, BA
Bridging roles (PM, Scrum Master) are often the ones doing the most manual data entry across systems
Client-facing roles (Account Manager, PM) often maintain shadow systems for client reporting

questions.text: How many different tools does someone need to switch between to complete their main workflow?
follow_ups: Which tool switches are the most frustrating?
Are there any integrations between these tools, or is it all manual?
hints: 3+ tool switches in a single workflow = high system switching waste
Common integration gaps: Jira ↔ PSA tool, HR tool ↔ PSA tool, PSA tool ↔ ERP
Manual integrations (copy-paste, re-keying) are the biggest source of data errors
Each tool switch is a potential data quality break point

phases.name: Data Creation
phases.description: Understand where and how data is born — the point of activity

questions.text: When work gets done (a story completed, a deliverable shipped, a milestone reached), how is that recorded?
follow_ups: Is the recording automatic (e.g., Jira status change) or manual (e.g., someone updates a spreadsheet)?
How quickly is it recorded — real-time, same day, end of week?
hints: Automatic recording (Jira transitions, Git commits) = high reliability, real-time
Manual recording (timesheet entry, status updates) = variable reliability, often delayed
The gap between 'work done' and 'work recorded' is a data freshness risk
End-of-week batch entry (common for timesheets) reduces granularity and accuracy

questions.text: How do your team members log their time? Walk me through the timesheet process.
follow_ups: Do they log against project codes, tasks, or both?
What's the typical delay between doing the work and logging the time?
hints: Time logging is the foundation of services firm financial data — if timesheets are wrong, everything downstream is wrong
Daily logging is ideal but rare. Weekly is common. Monthly is a data quality disaster
Dual time logging (Jira for tasks + PSA for billing) creates reconciliation headaches
Some firms log in 15-minute increments, others in half-days — granularity affects measure accuracy
Approval bottleneck: PMs who manage 5+ projects often batch-approve at month-end

questions.text: When a project changes scope or timeline, how is that captured and communicated?
follow_ups: Is there a formal change request process?
Does a scope change update the budget, or does the original budget remain?
hints: Scope changes without budget updates = hidden cost overruns
Change requests captured in email but not in the project tool = audit trail gap
The link between scope change → budget update → forecast revision is often broken
Some firms track change requests in Jira, others in SharePoint, others in email only

phases.name: Entities & Relationships
phases.description: Identify the core business objects and how they relate to each other

questions.text: Let's map the hierarchy: do you have accounts, programmes, and projects? Or just projects? How are they related?
follow_ups: Can a project belong to multiple programmes or accounts?
Is there a practice/capability/team dimension as well?
hints: Common hierarchy: Account → Programme → Project → Sprint/Phase
Some firms add: Practice/Capability (e.g., 'Data Engineering', 'UX Design') as a cross-cutting dimension
The hierarchy determines how financial data rolls up: project margin → programme margin → account margin
Resources may be allocated at project level but belong to a practice — creates a matrix

questions.text: How does a resource relate to a project? Is it a simple assignment, or are there phases, roles, and allocation percentages?
follow_ups: Can allocation change over the project lifecycle?
How do you handle people who work across multiple projects simultaneously?
hints: Resource-Project relationship often includes: role on project, allocation %, start/end dates, day rate
Multi-project allocation is the #1 pain point in services resource management
Some tools only support one project per person — leading to Excel shadow systems
The allocation vs actuals gap (planned 50% on Project A but only worked 30%) is a key management metric

phases.name: Pain Points & Workarounds
phases.description: Identify operational friction, manual effort, and shadow systems

questions.text: What's the most annoying thing your delivery teams have to do that isn't 'real work'? Think admin, reporting, data entry.
follow_ups: How much time per week does this take per person?
Has anyone tried to fix this? What happened?
hints: Timesheet entry across multiple systems is consistently the top complaint
Status reports that require compiling data from 3+ sources
Updating the same information in multiple places (Jira, PSA, Excel, client report)
Chasing approvals (timesheets, expenses, change requests)
Manual effort × number of people × frequency = total waste in hours/month

questions.text: If you could wave a magic wand and fix one data problem in your organisation, what would it be?
follow_ups: What's the impact of this data problem — cost, time, risk, or frustration?
Who else is affected by this problem?
hints: Common answers: 'accurate resource availability', 'real-time project financials', 'single source of truth for forecasts'
The magic wand question reveals the highest-impact improvement opportunity
Connect the answer back to the metrics chain: this data problem → affects this measure → distorts this metric → misleads this decision

typical_systems.name: Document Management
typical_systems.role: SOW storage, meeting notes, process documentation, templates
common_issues: Search is poor across large repositories

typical_systems.name: Reporting / BI
common_issues: Underlying data quality issues masked by visualisation

cross_perspective_connections.description: Revenue and margin calculations require approved timesheets and resource rates from management processes
cross_perspective_connections.suggested_question: How do approved timesheets flow into your revenue recognition and cost allocation?

cross_perspective_connections.description: Financial actuals originate from operational time logging and resource allocation
cross_perspective_connections.suggested_question: Where does the actual effort data come from that feeds your financial actuals?

cross_perspective_connections.description: Utilisation and capacity metrics depend on operational time logging and HR availability data
cross_perspective_connections.suggested_question: How does actual time worked (from timesheets) combine with availability (from HR) to calculate utilisation?

cross_perspective_connections.description: Management forecasts and pipeline data feed financial planning and revenue projections
cross_perspective_connections.suggested_question: How do project-level forecasts roll up into the financial forecast? Is it automatic or manual?

cross_perspective_connections.description: Sprint and delivery metrics from operations feed management's project health monitoring
cross_perspective_connections.suggested_question: How does sprint performance data flow into project RAG status and management reporting?

cross_perspective_connections.description: Timesheets are the primary data source for both billing/revenue and cost allocation
cross_perspective_connections.suggested_question: After timesheets are approved, how do they become revenue and cost entries in the financial system?

entity_patterns.description: Common entity structures found in professional services organisations

core_entities.name: Project
core_entities.description: A contracted engagement with a client, with defined scope, budget, and timeline

perspective_lenses.operational: A container for work — sprints, tasks, deliverables. What needs to be built and for whom
perspective_lenses.management: A unit of performance measurement — on time, on budget, delivering value. Where to focus attention
perspective_lenses.financial: A cost collector and revenue generator — P&L at the project level. Profitability unit

core_entities.name: Resource
core_entities.description: A person who delivers work on projects (employee or contractor)

perspective_lenses.operational: A worker with specific skills who executes tasks. What they can do and what they're working on
perspective_lenses.management: A capacity unit to be allocated and utilised. Are they fully booked? Right-skilled for demand?
perspective_lenses.financial: A cost item with a blended rate. People cost is the primary cost driver in services

core_entities.name: Account
core_entities.description: A client organisation that commissions projects

perspective_lenses.operational: The client context — their technology, their people, their way of working
perspective_lenses.management: A relationship to manage — satisfaction, growth potential, risk. Account health
perspective_lenses.financial: A revenue stream — total revenue, margin, lifetime value. Strategic value

core_entities.name: Timesheet
core_entities.description: A record of time worked by a resource on a project for a period

perspective_lenses.operational: A task I have to do — log my time accurately against the right codes
perspective_lenses.management: Compliance data — are people logging on time? Are hours reasonable? Approval needed
perspective_lenses.financial: Revenue and cost data — approved timesheets × rates = revenue/cost to post to GL

core_entities.name: Budget
core_entities.description: Financial envelope for a project — approved spend and forecast

perspective_lenses.operational: A constraint — we have this much budget, so scope accordingly
perspective_lenses.management: A tracking tool — are we on budget? What's the variance? Need to reforecast?
perspective_lenses.financial: A financial control — approved envelope, variance analysis, change request impact

core_entities.name: Lead / Opportunity
core_entities.description: A potential future project in the presales pipeline

perspective_lenses.operational: Future demand — we might need to staff this. What skills will it require?
perspective_lenses.management: Pipeline management — is it qualified? Who's pursuing it? What's the conversion likelihood?
perspective_lenses.financial: Future revenue — weighted pipeline value, revenue forecast impact, capacity planning input

core_entities.name: Programme
core_entities.description: A grouping of related projects under a client account, often with shared governance

perspective_lenses.operational: A scope boundary — projects in this programme share dependencies and resources
perspective_lenses.management: A governance unit — programme-level RAG, cross-project resource balancing
perspective_lenses.financial: A revenue/cost aggregation level between project and account

core_entities.name: SOW / Contract
core_entities.description: Statement of Work or contract defining scope, terms, and commercials

perspective_lenses.operational: The scope agreement — what we've committed to deliver
perspective_lenses.management: A commercial baseline — are we delivering within the agreed terms?
perspective_lenses.financial: A contractual commitment — revenue recognition basis, payment terms, invoicing schedule

core_entities.name: Risk
core_entities.description: An identified project or portfolio risk with likelihood and impact assessment

perspective_lenses.operational: A threat to delivery — what could go wrong and what's the contingency?
perspective_lenses.management: A portfolio concern — aggregate risk exposure, escalation trigger
perspective_lenses.financial: A financial exposure — potential cost impact, contingency budget requirement

core_entities.name: Licence / Tool
core_entities.description: A software licence or tool used in delivery or operations

perspective_lenses.operational: A tool I use daily — is it working? Do I have access?
perspective_lenses.management: An asset to manage — usage, renewals, right-sizing
perspective_lenses.financial: A cost line — total licence spend, cost per head, allocation to projects

common_relationships.description: Projects may be grouped into programmes
Resources are allocated to projects with role and percentage
Time is logged against project codes
Each project has a budget envelope
Leads come from existing or new accounts
SOWs define the commercial terms for projects

process_patterns.description: Common end-to-end processes in professional services organisations

processes.name: Lead to Project Pipeline
processes.description: From opportunity identification through presales to project kickoff
typical_steps: Capture Lead/Opportunity → Presales Estimate → Qualify & Assess → Create SOW → Set Up Project in Systems → Allocate Resources
key_pain_points: Presales estimates done in Excel, not connected to delivery tools
SOW creation is slow (legal review) — delays project start
Setting up project across 3+ systems (ERP, PSA, Jira) is manual and error-prone
Resource allocation requires checking availability across HR + PSA + Excel
processes.perspective_flow: management → management → management → management → management (with financial at SOW stage)

processes.name: Project Delivery Cycle
processes.description: Ongoing sprint-based or milestone-based delivery with status reporting
typical_steps: Sprint Planning → Execute Work → Submit Timesheets → Approve Timesheets → Update RAG Status → Produce Status Report → Update Forecast
key_pain_points: Status reports require manual compilation from 3+ sources (Jira + PSA + Excel)
RAG status is subjective — no objective criteria
Forecast updates are manual and done in Excel, not in the project tool
processes.perspective_flow: operational → operational → operational → management → management → management → financial

processes.name: Month-End Financial Close
processes.description: Monthly close including timesheet cutoff, actuals posting, and variance analysis
typical_steps: Close Timesheet Period → Post Actuals to GL → Variance Analysis → Compile Portfolio Report
key_pain_points: Timesheet approval bottleneck — PMs approve late, delaying close
Actuals lag — ERP posting takes days after cutoff
Variance analysis requires manual comparison of budget, forecast, and actuals from different systems
Portfolio report compilation takes 1-2 days of manual Excel/PowerPoint work

processes.name: Resource Allocation & Capacity Planning
processes.description: Matching resource supply to project demand
typical_steps: Review Capacity → Match Demand to Supply → Update Allocations → Review Costs
key_pain_points: Capacity data split across HR (leave) + PSA (allocation) + Excel (actual split)
Demand data comes from active projects + pipeline — different systems, different confidence levels
Multi-project allocation not supported by PSA tool — requires Excel workaround
Blended rates need regular review — new hires, rate changes, currency effects

measure_taxonomy.description: Standard measures used in professional services, organised by category

measures.name: Average Deal Size
measures.formula_pattern: Total Pipeline Value / Number of Deals

measures.name: Win Rate by Stage
measures.formula_pattern: Conversions at Stage / Entries at Stage

domain_vocabulary.description: Common terminology in professional services — helps the AI understand user language

terms.T&M: Time and Materials — billing model where client pays for actual hours at agreed rates
terms.Fixed Price: Billing model where client pays a fixed amount regardless of effort — risk sits with the provider
terms.Blended Rate: Average day rate across resource levels, used for simplified cost calculations
terms.SOW: Statement of Work — contractual document defining scope, deliverables, timeline, and cost
terms.PSA: Professional Services Automation — software for project, resource, and financial management
terms.RAG Status: Red/Amber/Green status indicator for project health
terms.Bench: Unallocated time — resources not assigned to billable projects
terms.Utilisation: Percentage of available time spent on billable work
terms.Pipeline: Future sales opportunities at various stages of qualification and negotiation
terms.Burn Rate: Rate of budget consumption over time
terms.Run Rate: Current spending extrapolated forward — what costs will be if nothing changes
terms.EAC: Estimate at Completion — current forecast of total project cost when finished
terms.ETC: Estimate to Complete — forecast of remaining cost from now to project end
terms.WIP: Work in Progress — work done but not yet billed or recognised as revenue
terms.Accrual: Financial adjustment to match revenue/costs to the period the work was performed
terms.Reforecast: Updated financial forecast based on latest information — typically monthly or quarterly
terms.Change Request: Formal request to modify project scope, timeline, or budget
terms.Demand: Future resource requirements from projects (active + pipeline)
terms.Supply: Available resource capacity after accounting for leave and existing allocations
terms.Backfill: Replacing a departing resource on a project with another person
terms.Ramp Up: Period when a new resource joins a project and is not yet fully productive
terms.FTE: Full-Time Equivalent — a measure of allocation (1 FTE = 100% of one person's time)
terms.Crystallisation: The moment when operational data becomes a frozen, trusted fact — e.g., timesheet approval crystallises hours for billing
